correctness.rationale: Distinct answers require injective signatures. Seven or fewer bits cannot encode 256 vertices. At eight bits a bijection would require 128 ones in each column, but a closed radius-three ball contains 1+8+28+56=93 vertices. At nine bits the total weight is 837; the exactly 256 words of weight at most four have total weight 837 and form the unique minimizing set (the next available words have weight at least five). Thus all those signatures are forced, and any two columns have 1+7+21=29 simultaneous ones. For distinct centers c,d, translation by c⊕d pairs points of the intersection without fixed points, so it has even size; with identical centers the intersection has size 93, not 29. Independent direct XOR enumeration of all 32,640 pairs of distinct centers (`python -B /workspace/branches/replay_records_1_3_4_5.py`, section 3) confirms the frozen table 93,58,58,38,38,20,20,0,0 by increasing distance including the identical case. The proof is for nonadaptive, fixed closed radius-three balls and gives only a lower bound; it does not supply a ten-ball system or determine the exact optimum. The erroneous arXiv identifier in reference 2 is bibliographic, not an input to the proof.

evidence: The Q7 radius-three case has a Fano-plane construction of seven separating balls; for the covered variant Kim et al. report eight. Katona's general separating theorem yields 256 log(256)/(93 log(e·256/93)), about 7.6. Janson–Laihonen give asymptotic identifying-code results with coverage.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The Q7 construction uses an odd-dimensional antipodal complement special to that case, and is not a Q8 lower bound. The general finite Katona bound only rounds up to eight here; asymptotic rates do not decide this finite equality obstruction.

evidence: In Q7, Kim et al. use uniform pair intersections as a necessary condition at the information-theoretic limit; in Q8, a nine-bit injection is not a bijection, so the condition of 29 does not follow from information capacity. It follows from saturating the minimum-weight nine-bit signature profile.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The general incidence bounds alone are insufficient; the extremal signature computation allows nine and needs the intersection obstruction to rule it out. A verified exact fixed-radius entry or a covering-identifying lower bound of at least 11 would change the prior-coverage assessment, but none was established in the passages read.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Separation permits exactly one empty signature at most. If I is the minimum additionally covering code size, then M≤I≤M+1: add the lone uncovered vertex as a center if necessary; adding a coordinate preserves uniqueness. The displayed introductory inequality in the arXiv text is inconsistent with its own Q7 example and is not used. To imply M≥10 by this reduction alone an identifying-code lower bound of at least 11 is needed.

originality.rationale: In the checked evidence, the near-half-radius Q7 construction and general uniform-size separating bounds do not yield the two extra queries at Q8. Requiring both uniqueness and coverage changes the problem; no inspected same-parameter covered-code result implies this lower bound. The new step beyond the signature weight bound is an equality-case incompatibility with Hamming-ball intersections. This is a bounded best-of-knowledge decision, not a historical priority claim.

value.rationale: Dimension eight at the same radius is the immediate neighbor of the information-theoretically sharp seven-query Q7 example. The bound rules out even a one-query overhead over the eight-bit capacity threshold; equal ball sizes alone do not rule out nine via the first moment. Rigidity of the extremal signature set and its incompatibility with Hamming-ball pair intersections give a substantive, checkable obstruction, without claiming the optimum.
